title: Mezzrow's Paris recordings, Panassie and Claude Bolling
summary: Welburn lists the sessions; Hugues Panassie sent for them and Claude Bolling mimicked many pianists.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Because apparently what happens here is that the Mezzrow recording session of November 1954 has Collins, and Claude Bolling is on piano.
Yes..

There's no bass player. Then in January in Paris in 1955, there is a recording. It is the same group, except that instead of one trumpet player, Lee Collins, there are two trumpet players. There's Wallace Davenport and Guy Lonome(?).
Yeah, there were ...(??)...
So you had two trumpet players and Jimmy Archey on trombone, but there's no bass player. Why was there no bass player, just for a matter of record? Mezzrow didn't want a bass player, or he didn't...?
Pops Foster, he was there, wasn't he?

It's possible, but Pops wasn't mentioned in this list here of people who were on the recordings. Maybe they neglected to mention him, I don't know. But there's no bass player listed. You played things like "Reverend
Moore (III) - 76
Blues"... Did you sing on that, "Reverend Blues"? No?
What's the name of it?
"Reverend Blues."
I don't know...
There's also "My Blue Heaven," "Coquette," "Careless Love."
Yes...

On the earlier session of the two, there's "Tiger Rag," "Basin Street Blues, "Squeeze Me," "When the Saints Go Marching In," "Tommy's Blues" and "Rockin' For Panassie," for Hugues Panassie. Was Hugues Panassie much...?
He was the one that sent for us to come over there.
He sent for you to come over. All right. Did he talk with a lot of the musicians?
Yes. He was born and raised in France.
Sure.

And he spoke very good English. He spoke French. He could talk to us, talk to the band in English. And Mezzrow could transport [sic] all we didn't understand... Mezzrow would transport [sic] it, you know, from him to us.
Moore (III) - 77
Translate it, okay. Now, who is Claude Bolling?

Claude Bolling was a piano player, a young boy during that time. He could play all different styles... I don't mean he don't play different styles. He played like a lot of different piano players from the States. He'd sound just like Claude Hopkins, some of him, some J.P. Johnson, Count Basie, Teddy Wilson -- sounded like them guys. Different things he'd do, he'd sound just like them.
Now, he's made some recordings recently, I think, that were put out...
Yeah, he was here in New York not very long ago. I didn't get to see him. I think he did a concert here with somebody. You know, I tried to find him, so we'd get... I was working someplace.
